show: „Starzyński” (Teatr Syrena, Warszawa; autorska premiera musicalowa Teatru Syrena). VERIFIED FACTS about this production — the synopsis must not contradict any of them: (1) The action is the evening, night and morning of 26 and 27 October 1939 — never 1941. Warsaw has capitulated and the German occupation has closed in; these are Starzynski's last hours in the city hall. (2) Official atmosphere: battered Warsaw, boundless helplessness, remorse, sadness and moral dilemmas; outside are ruins, autumn, the approaching Zaduszki (All Souls') and darkness; ghosts crawl out of memories and dream mixes with waking. It ends at the threshold of his arrest. (3) The production uses fragments of Adam Mickiewicz's 'Dziady', quotations from Starzynski's own speeches, and Ludwika Nitschowa's words from Polish Radio reportage; it is inspired by Grzegorz Piatek's biography 'Starzynski. Prezydent z pomnika'. (4) Do NOT give anyone a profession the sources do not state (Wladyslaw Studnicki was a political writer, not a critic). Stanislaw Lorentz was director of the Muzeum Narodowe. (5) Write flowing prose, NOT a cast list. Name only the few figures the story actually needs, and NEVER copy a cast-sheet entry with slashes in it (never write things like 'Ojciec/Józef Piłsudski', 'Paulina/Ludwika Nitschowa' or 'Sylwester Wojewódzki/Lech Niemojewski'). Do not enumerate the company.
synopsis:
Stefan Starzyński remains in his office at Warsaw’s City Hall as evening falls on 26 October 1939, a month after the city’s capitulation. The occupation has tightened around the battered capital, and he seems less to be working than enduring the final hours before the Germans come for him. Behind the walls, Stanisław Lorentz, director of the Muzeum Narodowe, is close at hand, while the city outside lies in ruins beneath autumn darkness and the approach of Zaduszki.

Throughout the night, Starzyński is drawn into an unstable realm where recollection, accusation and dream continually displace the present. His mother and father return; so do the women he loved, the obligations he accepted, and the choices that now demand an accounting. Władysław Studnicki emerges as a troubling voice from the past, while Syrena Warszawska gives the wounded city a mythic presence. Adam—at once a spectral companion and an echo of Mickiewicz’s world—draws Starzyński into confrontations that resemble both private confession and a national rite for the dead.

The City Hall becomes a place haunted by unfinished duties. Words once addressed to the people of Warsaw acquire new force and new ambiguity as Starzyński revisits the siege, the surrender, and the burden of having become an emblem of resistance. He cannot repair the ruined streets or protect everyone left in them; he can only decide how to meet the consequences of remaining. By the morning of 27 October, memories and visions recede just enough for the immediate danger to become unavoidable. The story stops on the threshold of his arrest.

The musical turns one man’s final night of freedom into a reckoning with responsibility, loss and the limits of heroic action. Its haunted Warsaw asks whether courage can coexist with remorse when survival itself has become a moral dilemma.
